sentences.text: This animal is classified as the species Acamptonectes densus, a member of the family Ophthalmosauridae.
It was estimated to reach a length of 3 meters, featuring a snout that was only 0.044 times as deep as it was long.

Its body possessed tightly fitting bones in the occiput and interlocking vertebral centra that made its trunk rigid, while its slender, ridged teeth were adapted for impaling soft, fleshy prey like fish and squid.
Despite having large eyes adapted for depth diving, the animal was likely a generalist predator, though its exact color remains unknown.
Acamptonectes was morphologically similar to the earlier ophthalmosaurines Ophthalmosaurus and Mollesaurus.
The genus and species were formally described by Fischer and colleagues in 2012, following the discovery of the first specimen in Speeton, England, in 1958.
The initial specimen was collected in 1958 by students and a technician from Hull University in the Speeton Clay Formation.
A partial subadult skeleton from Cremlingen, Germany, was also recognized as belonging to the genus.

A 2012 analysis found Acamptonectes grouped most closely with Ophthalmosaurus natans, but a 2019 analysis suggested it was closer to Janusaurus, Keilhauia, and Palvennia than to other ophthalmosaurines.
Acamptonectes lived during the Early Cretaceous, approximately 130 million years ago, with fossils recovered from Hauterivian strata in England and Germany.

Additional fossils were found in the Cambridge Greensand Formation in eastern England, dating to the late Albian or early Cenomanian, corresponding to the boundary between the Early and Late Cretaceous periods.

Researchers suggested the Hannover specimen might be a juvenile Acamptonectes based on the size and shape of its basicranium, while Ichthyosaurus brunsvicensis is considered a nomen dubium due to its fragmentary nature.

Researchers debated whether to resurrect the genus name Baptanodon for Ophthalmosaurus natans, but Fischer et al. rejected it due to homoplasy, and a 2019 analysis proposed a different phylogenetic arrangement for Acamptonectes within the Ophthalmosaurinae compared to earlier studies.
